This is a tutorial activity that will introduce you to the basics of R programming. It goes over running code and storing results, working with vectors, building and pulling pieces out of data frames, how folders and file paths work, and how to read a data file into R. It finishes with links for installing R on your own computer.

Every code box on this page runs, including the examples --- change them and re-run them if you want to see what happens. Nothing to install --- it all runs here in your browser. Click **Run** to run whatever is in the box, and **Check** when you think you've got it right. If you get stuck, **Show hint** will point you in the right direction. Your progress saves on this device, so you can stop partway and come back.

You should expect to spend around 10 minutes on this activity.

## 1. Running code

R is a calculator that remembers things. You type an expression, R evaluates it, and prints the answer. Try running the code below --- it's already complete, so just press **Run**.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="warmup" data-check="TRUE">
  <p class="rx-task">Press <strong>Run</strong>. The first one takes a few seconds to get going.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="2" spellcheck="false">2 + 2</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
</div>
```

The part that makes R useful is storing results. The arrow `<-` assigns a value to a name, and from then on that name stands in for the value.

```{=html}
<div class="rx-demo">
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="Example R code you can run and edit" rows="2" spellcheck="false">x &lt;- 10
x * 3     # 30</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
</div>
```

Names are case sensitive, can't start with a number, and shouldn't contain spaces. `mean_age` works; `Mean Age` doesn't.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex1" data-check='exists("answer") &amp;&amp; answer == 42'>
  <p class="rx-task">Replace the blank so that <code>answer</code> holds the number 42.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="2" spellcheck="false">answer &lt;- ____
answer</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>The blank is just the number itself: <code>answer &lt;- 42</code>.</p></div>
</div>
```

Most of the work in R happens through *functions*. A function has a name, and you give it input in parentheses. `sqrt(9)` returns 3, `round(3.14159, 2)` returns 3.14.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex2" data-check='exists("root") &amp;&amp; root == 8'>
  <p class="rx-task">Use a function to take the square root of 64 and store it in <code>root</code>.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="2" spellcheck="false">root &lt;- ____(64)
root</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>Square root is <code>sqrt</code>.</p></div>
</div>
```

## 2. Vectors

A single number isn't much use when you have 200 participants. R's basic container is the *vector*, which holds several values of the same type. You build one with `c()`, for "combine".

```{=html}
<div class="rx-demo">
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="Example R code you can run and edit" rows="2" spellcheck="false">ages &lt;- c(19, 22, 20, 25)
length(ages)   # 4</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
</div>
```

Functions like `mean()`, `sd()`, `min()` and `max()` take a whole vector and return one number. This is the part of R that makes it feel different from a spreadsheet: you describe what you want, not which cells to click.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex3" data-check='exists("scores") &amp;&amp; length(scores) == 4 &amp;&amp; mean(scores) == 7.5'>
  <p class="rx-task">Build a vector called <code>scores</code> holding 7, 9, 4 and 10, then take its mean.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="2" spellcheck="false">scores &lt;- ____(7, 9, 4, 10)
mean(scores)</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>The combine function is <code>c</code>, so the line starts <code>scores &lt;- c(</code>.</p></div>
</div>
```

## 3. Data frames

Real data has several variables at once, so vectors get stacked side by side into a *data frame*: rows are participants, columns are variables. This is what a dataset looks like in R.

You pull out one column with a dollar sign. If `participants` is the data frame and `age` is a column, then `participants$age` is the vector of ages, and you can hand that straight to `mean()`.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex4" data-check='exists("mean_age") &amp;&amp; mean_age == 21.5'>
  <p class="rx-task">Fill in the column name so <code>mean_age</code> is the average age.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="7" spellcheck="false">participants &lt;- data.frame(
  id = 1:4,
  age = c(19, 22, 20, 25),
  condition = c("control", "treatment", "control", "treatment")
)

mean_age &lt;- mean(participants$____)
mean_age</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>You want the <code>age</code> column, so <code>participants$age</code>.</p></div>
</div>
```

### Pulling pieces out with brackets

The dollar sign hands you a whole column. Square brackets let you ask for particular rows *and* particular columns, and the order inside the brackets is always rows first, then columns:

```{=html}
<div class="rx-demo">
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="Example R code you can run and edit" rows="5" spellcheck="false">participants &lt;- data.frame(id = 1:4, age = c(19, 22, 20, 25))

participants[2, ]        # row 2, every column
participants[, "age"]    # every row, just the age column
participants[2, "age"]   # row 2 of the age column</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
</div>
```

Leaving a slot empty means "give me all of them". The comma does the work here, so `participants[2, ]` and `participants[, 2]` ask for completely different things --- the second row versus the second column.

If you can remember **RC Cola**, you can remember the order: **R**ows, then **C**olumns.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex5" data-check='exists("third_age") &amp;&amp; third_age == 20'>
  <p class="rx-task">Fill in the blank so <code>third_age</code> is the age of the third participant.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="4" spellcheck="false">participants &lt;- data.frame(id = 1:4, age = c(19, 22, 20, 25))

third_age &lt;- participants[____, "age"]
third_age</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>RC Cola: rows first. You want row 3, so <code>participants[3, "age"]</code>.</p></div>
</div>
```

Useful first moves with any new data frame: `nrow()` for the number of rows, `names()` for the column names, `head()` for the first few rows, and `summary()` for a quick description of every column.

## 4. Folders and file paths

This is where people usually get stuck, and it has nothing to do with statistics.

R is always sitting in some folder, called the *working directory*. When you ask it to open a file, it looks starting from there. `getwd()` tells you where you are.

An *absolute* path spells out the location from the root of your computer, like `/Users/you/Documents/lab-study/data/responses.csv`. It works on your machine and nobody else's. A *relative* path starts from the working directory instead --- `data/responses.csv` --- and keeps working when you send the folder to me, which is why we use relative paths for everything.

So we keep each study in one self-contained folder:

```{=html}
<div class="rx-tree">lab-study/
├── lab-study.Rproj      the project file; opening it sets the working directory
├── data/
│   └── responses.csv    raw data, never edited by hand
├── scripts/
│   └── analysis.R       the code
└── output/
    └── figure-1.png     things the code produces</div>
```

Open `lab-study.Rproj` and R's working directory becomes `lab-study/`, so `data/responses.csv` points at the right file on any computer. `file.path()` joins the pieces with the right separator, which is how you avoid the slash-versus-backslash problem between Mac and Windows.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex6" data-check='exists("path") &amp;&amp; path == "data/responses.csv"'>
  <p class="rx-task">Fill in the folder name so <code>path</code> is <code>"data/responses.csv"</code>.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="2" spellcheck="false">path &lt;- file.path("____", "responses.csv")
path</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>Look at the tree above: the file sits in the <code>data</code> folder.</p></div>
</div>
```

## 5. Reading in data

Once the path is right, reading a CSV is one line. `read.csv()` takes a path and hands back a data frame.

There's a real file waiting at `data/responses.csv` in this browser session: eight participants, with `id`, `age`, `condition` and `score` columns.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex7" data-check='exists("responses") &amp;&amp; nrow(responses) == 8'>
  <p class="rx-task">Read the file in, then look at the first few rows.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="3" spellcheck="false">responses &lt;- read.csv("data/responses.csv")

head(responses)</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>This one's already complete --- just press <strong>Run</strong>, then <strong>Check</strong>.</p></div>
</div>
```

`head()` prints the column names along the top, which is usually how you find out what you're actually working with. Now pull one of those columns out and summarise it.

```{=html}
<div class="rx" data-id="ex8" data-check='exists("avg_age") &amp;&amp; round(avg_age, 2) == 21.75'>
  <p class="rx-task">Fill in the column name so <code>avg_age</code> is the average age of the eight participants.</p>
  <textarea class="rx-code" aria-label="R code for this exercise" rows="4" spellcheck="false">responses &lt;- read.csv("data/responses.csv")

avg_age &lt;- mean(responses$____)
avg_age</textarea>
  <div class="rx-bar">
    <button class="rx-btn rx-run" type="button">Run</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-check" type="button">Check</button>
    <button class="rx-btn rx-secondary rx-hint-btn" type="button">Show hint</button>
    <span class="rx-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></span>
  </div>
  <pre class="rx-out" role="status" aria-live="polite" hidden></pre>
  <div class="rx-hint" hidden><p>Run the chunk above to see the column names. The one you want is <code>age</code>.</p></div>
</div>
```

If a `read.csv()` call fails, the problem is almost always the path rather than the file. Check `getwd()` first, then check the spelling.

## 6. Getting R on your own computer

The browser version is a teaching tool. For actual work you want both of these, installed in this order:

1. **[R](https://cloud.r-project.org/)** --- the language itself.
2. **[RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)** --- the editor most people use to write R. Free, and it expects R to already be there.

Then make a project rather than a loose script: in RStudio, **File → New Project → New Directory**, and lay it out like the tree in section 4.

If you want to keep going before we talk, [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) is free online and is where I'd start.
